newsitem.title: USA: Summer reading -- considering business tales.
newsitem.headline: Summer reading -- considering business tales.

text.p: A visit to a bookstore would offer a wealth of how-to books on running a small business, but you might get more insightful and gripping accounts in aisles far away from the business section -- books you might want to take on vacation, like I did.

Take the classics. At the behest of a close friend, who happens to be a college English professor, I picked up George Eliot's "The Mill on the Floss," thinking the Victorian classic would be a pleasant diversion.

Though it was a bit dense at first, I was soon gripped by a riveting account whose plot turned on a family business gone haywire. Little did I know that the novel would offer a cautionary tale on family debt.

The story is about the coming of age of Maggie Tulliver, a young girl whose passions get the better of her. But what I found fascinating was her family's economic circumstances, which Eliot takes pains to describe.

The novel was published in 1860, but the tale could well be about any small family business today that made the mistake of borrowing money from relatives and then got hammered by a bad business decision.

Maggie's father, Mr. Tulliver, is a well-meaning mill owner on the river Floss. But he relies on credit from his wife's family, who tends to look down on him as a social inferior. He in turn lends money to his destitute sister, who lives on a farm with a hard-working husband and gaggle of kids.

Tulliver is able to service this family debt until he makes a fatal mistake. A proud man, he becomes convinced that a wealthy lawyer in town is diverting water from his mill. He files a lawsuit, which drags on for years, and ultimately loses, saddling him with huge legal bills.

His relatives, of course, are critical and tightfisted. Although desperate for money, he cannot bring himself to force his poor sister to sell all her livestock to pay back his loan. The result -- he looses control of the mill to the adversary he sued, and is stricken with illness brought on by his failure.

Maggie's brother Tom is forced to drop out of school, enter business and try to earn enough money to pay off the debts. Adept and eager, he prospers, pays off the family bills, restores its tattered reputation and buys back the mill.

If it sounds like a happy ending, it isn't. But I won't give it away; suffice it to say that the book can be read as a tale about the perils of a family business, the risks of relying on relatives for money and the dangers of legal battles.
That last point -- about the risks and costs entailed in pursuing suits -- was driven home in a contemporary book, "A Civil Action," by Johathan Harr, which also occupied a quiet summer weekend.

The book was first published two years ago, but I recently got the paperback edition (as a birthday present). Thinking the book might be a pleasant vacation read, I found myself gripped to the point of frustration, unable to put it down, even to enjoy the hiking trails in the Rocky Mountains.

A legal-environmental thriller, the book is a disturbing account of a lawyer's battle against two corporations whose chemicals, he believes, seeped into the water supply of Woburn, Mass., causing abnormally high rates of disease and death.

The lawyer, Jan Schlichtmann, is obsessed with winning the suit and righting a wrong. But the battle is so costly that he drives his firm deep into debt, loses his condominium and Porche, and is eventually driven nearly mad by the fight.
Despite the fact that nearly all the evidence backs him up, he still must battle an apparently reluctant federal judge and two deep-pocketed adversaries.
Business owners often talk about the need for passion in pursuing their goals, but this suit amounts to an obsession -- one that Schlictmann pursues beyond any rational consideration of risk.
His partner warns him that the suit is a black hole, but despite the misgivings, he digs ever deeper into the bottomless pit and the suit that drags on for years.

I won't reveal the cliffhanger ending, but the lawyer ends up penniless on a beach in Hawaii, and, according to the afterword, stays there for several years. Woburn, meanwhile, was the subject of a costly clean-up.
Schlichtmann seems like the quintessential entrepreneur, taking unbelievable risks to try and achieve the end he desires. But in this case, the business becomes personal.

Taken on its own, no lawyer -- or business person -- would have battled the way Schlichtmann did, taken the risks he did or pursued the case to the end. But that was the price of his passion, perhaps the type of irrational flailing that is needed to take on the big guys.

(Samuel Fromartz is a Washington-based journalist who writes frequently about entrepreneurs and emerging companies. He can be reached by email at sam1on1 (at) aol.com. Any opinions expressed here are his own).
